#3231. The Man Who Broke the Texas Democratic Party to Save It

T he personal office of Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder is a museum to Democrats’ greatest victories, disappointments, close calls, and one-hit wonders.

“He’s a crazy motherfucker that guy,” Katherine Fischer, executive director at Texas Majority PAC, quips to me as I sift through boxes of what I estimate to be several thousand vintage (and not so vintage) campaign pins, trying to be mindful of old rusty needles. “In the best possible way,” she clarifies.

Buttons reading “UNBEATABLE MONDALE FERRARO,” “SHIRLEY CHISHOLM FOR PRESIDENT,” and “Smile If You Had an Affair with Bill Clinton” flow across the conference table like spilled gold from an overturned pirate’s chest. Every available flat plane of space from which something can be hung or displayed in the Dallas office is occupied. A collection of ceramic Jim Beam whiskey decanters shaped like Democratic donkeys lives behind his desk. Ashtrays full of lapel pins dot tables and shelves. An entry table holds a gavel belonging to former House Speaker Sam Rayburn, a true blue son of Texas. Campaign posters for Lyndon Baines Johnson — Scudder’s favorite president — Robert Kennedy, Barbara Jordan, FDR, Hubert Humphrey, Jimmy Carter, Barack Obama, and dozens of others form a crowded gallery wall spanning the length of the room. The closets are stuffed with storage bins containing money stacks of political bumper stickers and rolled poster boards. A “Frances Farenthold for Governor” sign is displayed above the toilet in the bathroom.

It is the lair of a political mad scientist, one whose experiment just came alive.

A Democratic senator from Texas is headed to Washington, D.C. A Democrat is going to be the governor. A Democrat is going to be lieutenant governor. The party also flipped the seats of the attorney general, comptroller, agricultural commissioner, land commissioner, and railroad commissioner. They converted 12 judicial seats from red to blue, took over the board of education for the first time in three decades, and won control of the Texas state House for the first time since 2002.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The transformation may feel like an overnight fluke to outside onlookers, with the party riding a wave of anti-Trump sentiment into a generational electoral coup. To think that would require discounting the work of extremely sophisticated candidate campaigns, organizers, and the work Scudder began to ensure that any gains made by Texas Democrats — however marginal — could serve as a foundation rather than a transitory win.

Six-foot-three with a large frame, dark hair, and bright hazel eyes, Scudder can cut a mean figure if he has the inclination to. When he’s not stumping, soliciting, or selling, he can be goofy, prone to bouts of excess energy, and eager to discuss the project he’s thrown himself into over the last 20 months: a radical reconfiguration of the Texas Democratic Party.

As chair of the party, he’s angered longtime fixtures of the state’s political establishment, grated on the political economy of the region, and ultimately — through both accident and intent — placed Democrats in a near-perfect position to meet the moment when lighting finally struck.

It’s now a blue Texas, if he can keep it.

“I am quite literally the most partisan man in the state of Texas,” Scudder — a golden pin of a red-eyed donkey in boxing gloves glistening on his lapel — laughs over a tray of brisket. Elected the chair of the Texas Democratic Party in 2025 for what was initially only a partial term, Scudder now finds himself at the center of what generations of Democrats in the Lone Star State dreamed of every time they cast a ballot: a viable state party, with control of the levers of power, and political capital to spend. Related Content Rod Wave Indicted for Allegedly Carrying Oxycodone and a Gun While Speeding Travis Scott and Don Toliver Sued for Copyright Infringement Over 2019 Hit 'What to Do?' Thomas Markle Facing New Child Sex Abuse Charges in the Philippines Fingers Point to RFK Jr. as U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status

“People kept saying you’re doing too much, too fast, you’re supposed to be a caretaker chair, you’re going to lose all this institutional knowledge,’” Scudder says in his Texarkana brogue that broadcasts his rural roots — when we first met at Terry Black’s Barbecue in Austin. “You’re worried I’m going to ruin the institutional knowledge of what? Losing?”

Veteran organizers, current as well as former Texas politicians, and advisers described the Texas Democratic Party of their lifetimes as a bloated, Austin-centric social club that did little for candidates, and even less for voters. The party was caught in a cyclical spiral of self-defeatism, and — through a combination of financial and structural factors — unable to retain and grow insurgent waves of voter support like that which boosted former U.S. Rep. Beto O’Rourke’s near-miss in the 2018 Senate race. After the losses of 2024, particularly among Hispanic and Black voters within the state, Lone Star Democrats found themselves in a crisis.

Democrats “thought you could lock a bunch of consultants in a room in Austin and buy your way out of the problem,” Scudder tells me, after (correctly) complaining that charging $50 for a tray of brisket and sides is ridiculous. Scudder, himself from a farming family, does not abide by sacred cows. His first three major actions upon assuming the chairmanship were to move the party headquarters out of the liberal stronghold of Austin to red-ringed Dallas County, clear the debt weighing down their accounts, and overhaul the party’s leadership.

The leadership overhaul almost derailed his tenure just as it began. Top staffers, including the party’s former chief of staff and executive director, resigned after Scudder announced they would be required to move to the new Dallas headquarters, accusing him of wanting to remain in his hometown (the Austin office was converted to a field office). Claims of union-busting and racism were leveled against him by former party employees, two of whom ultimately attempted to unseat him when he ran for a full term in the summer of this year. By then, Scudder had managed to bring enough of the party around to his vision to comfortably secure his reelection to a four-year term.

“When I came in the party had about a third of its precinct chairs full across the whole state, and about 20 percent of our counties didn’t even have a county chair. We needed to rebuild it.”

Scudder launched a widespread organizer and candidate development effort to establish a presence in all 254 Texas counties, the party surged recruitment and pulled in over 100 candidates to fill out downballot races — many of which hadn’t had a Democrat run in years — through the “Texas Challengers” program. For the first time in the party’s modern history, every race had a candidate. Now-outgoing Governor Greg Abbott and his advisers dismissed the effort as a “gimmick” earlier this year. A dozen of them would go on to win.

Texas Democrats staffed up over a thousand county and precinct chairs, and moved to open field offices in Houston, Eagle Pass, and Amarillo. The party rolled out paid civics education classes to boost voter turnout, and enforced a new, equal-opportunity bidding process for campaign consultants and services, negotiating universal rates to save candidates millions in expenditures across the state. They also built the first coordinated campaign in the party’s history, pulling together over $40 million in campaign contributions statewide, including a research consortium available to local candidates typically excluded from the multi-billion-dollar consultant and pollster economy. Fischer, who oversaw the coordinated campaign with Texas Majority PAC, told me that almost immediately after Scudder’s election “we started to build the machine that would be used in 2026,” with limited funds and a lot to prove, the partnership focused on “efficiency and creativity,” to make every dollar work for the party.

The way Scudder and his staff tell it, it was the beginning of a 10-year plan, maybe five or six if they managed to do every single thing right. To them, a great night in the midterms would have been one that sent James Talarico to the Senate, flipping a few House seats, and maybe even stealing the governorship. Roughly a week before the election, Scudder received a polling update from the research consortium, predicting blowout wins throughout the state. “I looked up at the team,” he recalled, “and said ‘fuck the consortium is busted.”

In early 2025, Scudder invited his wife, Carly — a specialized therapist for foster children — to his office. The couple were expecting their first child later that year, and he had a pitch to make.

On one side of a freestanding dry erase board, he had a bulleted list of “all the things we wanted in a name.” A name that wasn’t weird or exceedingly common, worked with Carly’s mother’s maiden name (Joiner) as a middle name, and ideally a reference to a family name.

“I walked her through it,” he gushed, reenacting how he flipped over the board for her, and there in large letters was his proposal: LYNDON JOINER SCUDDER — after the 36th president of the United States, a born and bred Texan, and also an amalgamation of her full name — Carolyn — and her father’s name, Don. “We couldn’t name him Don,” he adds in a conspiratorial whisper.

Little Lyndon — now 15 months old and completely unaware of what just happened in his his state — was born last July.

LBJ clearly looms large for Scudder. He’s not only a symbol of the true power of progressive Texan governance, but of the power elected officials ultimately have to shape the lives of those they govern.

“Johnson’s Great Society pulled my family out from poverty,” he says. Born in East Texas near the not-so-new town of New Boston, Scudder’s family carved a path to their American dream on the winds of the Democratic social policies of the 20th century. His grandfather was delivered alone by his mother “in a wash bucket” on the family farm that, as he claims, only had water and electricity because of FDR. The programs of the New Deal and Great Society would rescue the Scudders from the fallout of the Great Depression. His left hand sports a gold wedding band, his right an edgeworn class ring from Sam Houston State University, the word “honor” engraved inside the band. He was the first person in his family to go to college, and it “might as well have been Harvard.”

“Everything I have in my life is because progressive Democrats,” he insists. “Democrats were the only people fighting for me. I love this party, and to think that Republicans could get elected, get rid of such a rich history of this progressivism in this country, and just run them up the way they did — I have no fucking patience.”

That patience began to run out at around 12 years old. In the early 2000s Republicans would seize same sex marriage and relationships — in a similar manner as they now treat anti-trans issue — as a supposed social contagion with which to browbeat the opposition. Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), then the state attorney general, defended anti-sodomy laws criminalizing same-sex couples, and the party at large sought to brand LGBTQ individuals as unfit to parent. Scudder, the child of a lesbian couple, took to door knocking in opposition.

He became an organizer for Texas College Democrats and Texas Young Democrats, opening dozens of chapters throughout the state. His own attempts at seeking elected office fell flat — losing a Texas state Senate race to Republican incumbent Bob Hall in 2018, and a Democratic primary to Texas House Rep. John Bryant, a former member of the U.S. House of Representatives, in 2022. It is perhaps a testament to Scudder’s graciousness that Bryant has since become a close friend and adviser, so much so that he officiated his wedding.

Perhaps the most revolutionary thing about Scudder is his lack of cynicism. Losing doesn’t scare him, losers don’t disgust him. “I know where all the landmines are because I’ve stepped on them all,” he jokes at one point as we stand in among his collection of decades of campaign shrapnel. All the names of victors, legends, disappointments, and “what ifs” piled together into a movement he can now shape.

Almost everything in Jim Hightower’s home looks like it was brought into the world by human hands. The ranch-style house in a quiet Austin neighborhood just off of South Congress is full of things that were carved, woven, pinched, molded, and whittled. It’s the kind of lived-in western space the tech transplants of the Austin goldrush pay out the ass for, but never really achieve. Outside, his garden is an untamed tangle of native plants and wildflowers. At 83, he likes that they “basically take care of themselves.” Voters, not so much.

Hightower is a bit of a legend among those who know political ball. As a younger man he worked under Texas Senator Ralph Yarborough — a staunch supporter of integration and civil rights during a time when most Southern senators refused to do so. He founded the progressive newspaper The Texas Observer and served as Texas Agriculture Commissioner between 1983 to 1991 — the last Democrat to hold the office until Clayton Tucker was elected last week. He is now one of the only living members of the last generation of Texas Democrats to serve in statewide elected office — one that held power during a time when the party represented union labor, farm workers, and social and economic advancement for the diverse population of the state.

“Populism began in Lampasas, Texas. Literally four farmers sitting around a kitchen table saying the banks are screwing us, and the railroads are screwing us, and we’ve got to do something,” he explains to me as we chat on his screened-in back porch. Somewhere along the way, as corporate interest and big money took hold of American politics, “our party quit standing for worker rights, environmentalism as strongly as we had. We still ostensibly stood for it but we lacked conviction and we lacked action, and people noticed that.”

When Hightower ran for Agricultural Commissioner— alongside future governor Ann Richards, then a candidate for State Treasurer — the candidates ran as a collective ticket, a “unified campaign” that built on their individual constituencies. “They thought they couldn’t win, and here we came,” Hightower recalls. It wasn’t “just one ego, but an actual progressive movement that could change Texas.”

It’s a romantic vision of a time long gone, but it rhymes with the Democratic victory of 2026. In the aftermath of 2024, with Texas Democrats once solid multi-racial coalition in shambles, it was clear something needed to change. As the party looked to make inroads in the state in 2026, O’Rourke advised Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa to treat her run as a joint venture with the party’s Senate candidate, arguing that it would be near impossible for a single Democrat to pull off the upset without building a multi-candidate voter coalition. Quality candidates with robust campaigns could make the jump under the right set of circumstances, in the right cycle — but making the party a true competitive force long term would require specialized attention. “We were looking for a party chair who could do something besides sit there in the chair,” Hightower says. Scudder, adept at fundraising and a wunderkind communicator, seemed like a viable choice. “He was willing to fight the bullshit and the bullshitters who were retarding the party, who didn’t seem to even quite understand what the party was and what it could be.”

The people who work with Scudder will tell you that he’s kind of crazy, a bit gregarious, a font of boundless energy that sometimes needs to be reined in and is smart enough to know it. He will readily hand out his phone number to anyone who asks for it, take any call, respond to whatever request comes from whatever part of the state. Lillian Salerno, a senior adviser to Scudder and former Obama administration official, met him when he was 19 years old.

After years favoring corporate Democrats, Scudder wanted to create a culture where “when candidates came in, they felt recognized” by the party, Salerno tells me over coffee near the Texas Capitol. She had run and lost a House race in 2018, and knew firsthand how the process feels for a candidate. “It didn’t work out for me — but I didn’t feel like the party gave a shit whether I ran or not,” she says. “Maybe it was just my impression, but I felt like I wasn’t an Austin person, so I didn’t really have a place. If I felt like that, maybe other candidates did too.”

Scudder’s opening blitz was about as subtle as a gunfight, but it served to (mostly) reset the decayed relationships between the party core and the state at large.

The party “was always asking me for a contribution, as opposed to doing anything that I felt was particularly meaningful to get me elected,” says Texas House Rep. John Bryant. “Under Kendall, it’s completely different, and a lot of the elected officials are having to come around to this realization.”

“In my experience the county chairs of the staff had just clashed endlessly, they couldn’t stand each other,” Terri Burke, the current Executive Director of the party, tells me over Diet Cokes in Scudder’s office, which is separate from the main party headquarters because (as he will readily tell you) he can be a bit overwhelming. “The State Democratic Executive Committee (SDEC), they couldn’t stand the staff. The staff couldn’t stand them. There was so much conflict. There was so much dysfunction.”

And not just dysfunction, but a refusal to adapt. “We’ve been doing the same old, same old for a long time, but not getting the results that we all of us wanted to see,” says Texas state Senator Royce West — a power broker and longtime fixture in the Texas political scene. “Yes, there were some controversial decisions that were being made. But here’s the deal: sometimes you’ve got to be a disruptor. And if you’re going to be a disruptor, it has to be done with the purpose. Kendall is the person to do it.”

As goes Texas politically, so goes America

Scudder is quite young compared to most of Texas’ Democratic greats. During our first meeting in Austin, Scudder, still a little scrambled by the outcome of election night, mentions that there was not a single living Texas Democratic Party chair who knew how to actually plan a gubernatorial inauguration. He was going to be flying blind.

Getting Gina Hinojosa sworn in is a small task compared to the plans Scudder is already brewing for 2028 and beyond. Democrats made history, now his job is to retain their control of the state, and ideally expand it.

“I gotta protect all these flips. I gotta flip a couple Senate seats,” he rattles off at one point. “If you think I’m not going after that Senate next cycle you haven’t met me yet.”

Scudder also intends to do all he can to ensure Democrats govern as Democrats. There’s a lot of talk at the moment of concession-making and what sort of limits Hinojosa and other Democrats should abide by in order to avoid rattling the temporarily dormant Republican coalition in the state. Scudder sees part of his job as ensuring the coalition doesn’t give up the shop.

“We just want to be helpful, but part of that being helpful is understanding that it’s a Democratic governor, and we would expect her to stay as close to the Democratic platform as we could possibly get,” he says. “People got her elected as a Democrat, and we would like for her to govern as such.”

They’re up against immense challenges. There will not be a major statewide candidate on the ballot in 2028, which means their efforts will be attached entirely to the presidential ticket. Republicans in the state have already broadcast their intent to throw wrenches into Hinojosa’s tenure wherever they can. He will have to convince the national Democratic party that Texas is no longer a state that they can afford to write off.

We are “responsible for a movement” now, he says. Our “job is to grow it.”

Should he succeed where his predecessors have failed, the implications go far beyond Texas.

One of the first people to call Scudder and congratulate him after election night was Senator Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who has advised the chair on his organizing efforts, and frequently campaigns on behalf of Texas candidates.

“As goes Texas politically, so goes America,” Sanders tells me over the phone, noting that the trove of Electoral College votes harbored by the state would make presidential math near impossible for Republicans. “What happened on November 3 is extraordinarily important, not just for Texas but for America — and Kendall, in a very quiet way, helped make that happen by demanding that there be candidates in every race, every legislative seat in in the state, and by building the kind of grassroots movement that should be built not only in Texas but all over the country.”

“There is no reason why [Texas] should not be one of the more progressive states in the country,” the senator adds. “It’s a young state, it’s a working class state, large minority populations — there was no rational reason why it was run by right-wing leaders — and I think that’s something that Kendall understood in what he did.”  Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage

Making Texas a true swing state or returning it to a true blue stronghold, would be the political feat of the century.

Scudder is not taking his eye off the ball. “It’s one thing to burn their house down,” he tells me with a hungry glint in his expression. “But I want to nail their door shut.”

#3227. Apple hears Liquid Glass feedback, tests small but welcome change

Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale.

Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling …

What am I supposed to be looking at here?

Are we talking about the barely-noticeable fade at the top of the screen?

Apple’s introduction of the Liquid Glass UI split the Apple community, some hailing it as one of the best improvements seen for many years, and others rejecting it as a usability disaster.

As is often the case with any change, the controversy dampened significantly once people had a chance to get used to it. That is not the same as everyone being happy with it, however. Apple later tried to please most of the people most of the time with a slider that allows people to customize the level of transparency, from a very frosted glass look to an almost completely clear one.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted that the company is currently testing a small but welcome additional choice.

The difference is somewhat subtle, and some may consider it irrelevant, but as someone who has transparency maxed-out I’m a fan of the softer fade and would welcome the option to be able to reinstate this.

#3226. The Irresistible Alchemy of Man / Woman / Chainsaw

W hatever you do, do not ask the six musicians in Man/Woman/Chainsaw which one of them is the chainsaw.

“Don’t do it,” warns singer Vera Leppänen, looking deadly serious. “We’ve heard that one so many times.”

“It’s so annoying,” says her bandmate Billy Doyle, shaking his head.

Billy Ward, another bandmate, agrees: “Don’t ask about the name.”

Luckily, the name is far from the most interesting thing about this fast-rising, fantastically original London group. Their first full-length album, Cannonball, collides all kinds of sounds that really shouldn’t go together — vulnerable folk, head-banging hard rock, a bit of classical, a little dance music, several genuinely enormous pop hooks — and, somehow, it works like a charm every single time. It’s a magic trick that gets more remarkable with every replay. When we saw Man/Woman/Chainsaw play at South By Southwest in March 2025, we called them “a young band in the process of inventing something ecstatically new.” Cannonball is what they invented, and sure enough, it’s one of this year’s most rewarding debuts.

The day after their first-ever New York show, the six of them have gathered in the backyard of a coffee shop in Bed-Stuy to chat with Rolling Stone. It’s our second choice for a meeting spot — the first café we tried had no room for a party of seven — but these young musicians are hardly bothered by a last-minute change of location. Leppänen (lead vocals and bass), Ward (lead vocals and guitar), Emmie-Mae Avery (lead vocals and keyboard), Clio Starwood (violin), Doyle (guitar), and Lola Cherry (drums), all aged 21, sit around a table in the sun, lighting rollies, laughing, and trading notes on last night’s gig.

“It’s funny,” Leppänen says. “America’s so far away for us, and they know our songs.”

“The music crossed the pond,” says Starwood.

“Yeah,” Ward says. “I walked past some people chatting at the bar, and they were talking about why they were there: ‘So I’m a really big Chainsaw fan…'” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

A few hours later, at the second stop on their U.S. tour, they show why their music has drawn such an enthusiastic audience in this country. It’s the night before Halloween, and the club is packed with costumed people who are ready to have fun — and Man/Woman/Chainsaw are more than happy to oblige. Up front, Ward and Leppänen rage like a pair of punk-rock demon twins. He growls theatrically on “The Thing” and “Goddamn, Lizard Man!,” and she slides with ease from the sullen fury of “Still Angry” to the pristine clarity of “Lighter.” Starwood shreds on her violin, Doyle brings a dash of jazzy style on guitar, and Cherry is a tireless dynamo behind the kit. Then there’s Avery, whose mellifluous vocals are indispensable to “Nosedive” — their biggest hit by far, with nearly 2.5 million Spotify plays — and their killer cover of the Breeders’ “Cannonball.” By the end of the night, the whole room is literally jumping.

Man/Woman/Chainsaw have been building toward this moment for about seven years. Ward and Leppänen were the first to meet, crossing paths at age 14 at the BRIT School, the performing-arts laboratory whose alumni include Adele, Amy Winehouse, Lola Young, and Olivia Dean. They spent the next few years assembling a backing band, which wasn’t too hard — “We knew a lot of people that played a lot of instruments,” Leppänen says — and booking gigs at local pubs. Related Content Who Gets to Own Rock & Roll History? No One Writes About Everyday Life Quite Like Star Moles How Bob Dylan’s Trip to London Inspired ‘Girl From the North Country’ Geese Never Thought They’d End Up Here

“We’d be in school, and Billy and Vera would come up to me at lunch and be like, ‘Do you want to go play the fucking Amersham Arms tonight?'” Avery recalls.

By the time they all turned 16 or 17, they were drawing attention for their wild live performances. (The band name, for the record, appears to be a reference to feminist film critic Carol J. Clover’s influential 1992 volume Men, Women, and Chainsaws, in which she identified the horror trope of the “final girl.”) And though Ward dismisses the music they were making at this point as “just noisy London bullshit,” they found a place in a scene that was regaining its bearings after the end of Covid restrictions.

“It’s such a privilege to be from a city that has so many venues, that has so many people that champion independent music,” Leppänen says. “We were very lucky to be able to just go out and do whatever.”

“We’d be on lineups with crazy noise rock, or post-punky stuff with a guy talking, or really electronic stuff,” Ward says. “There’s just such a variety.”

“It felt like you could do anything,” Cherry says.

Man/Woman/Chainsaw’s eclectic sound reflects the band’s democratic writing style, where anyone can make a suggestion and everyone will listen. It’s “the cocktail combination of six brains,” as Starwood puts it. And while many of them are fond of pop acts like Chappell Roan, Olivia Rodrigo, and Lana Del Rey, they see no contradiction between those sounds and the others in their mix.

“A lot of the best rock music, even the artiest, weirdest, guitary-est music, has great pop choruses,” Ward says. “That’s a thing that pretty universally makes the song good, is having something you can come back to. It’s important.”

They spent about two years workshopping the songs on Cannonball before stepping into RAK Studios with producers Seth Evans and Margo Broom in the summer of 2025 to begin recording. All the while, most of them were attending university (all but Ward and Avery, who opted to focus on the band). As part of her degree, Leppänen wrote papers on subjects including the Irish rap trio Kneecap, for a class on music and politics. She mentions that she later met one of the members of that group — “I did tell him I wrote about him. He said, ‘You’re welcome.’ And he said I was charming” — which leads her to a story about the time they all ran into Lewis Capaldi at a Chainsaw show. “He said I was a boss,” she says.

“Both of these people were wasted when they gave these compliments,” Ward observes wryly. “So let’s take it with a pinch of salt.”

For another graduating requirement, Leppänen submitted a performance by Man/Woman/Chainsaw. “If people want to know if we’re a good band, the answer is yeah, we got a good mark,” says Starwood.

Some of the songs on the album began with a group jam, like “Only Girl,” the soaring anthem that opens Cannonball. “I just had two chords,” Ward says. “And a dream,” Leppänen says.

“We could tell that was going to be the first song on the album as soon as we wrote it,” Cherry adds. “When it feels right, you can tell, because we just want to play the song again and again and again.”

Others emerged more fully-formed, like “Still Angry,” which came from a voice note that Leppänen sent the band. “I played it to my mom,” Ward says. “I was like, ‘Listen to this shit. It’s a fucking amazing pop song. Vera’s done it again.'”

“Nosedive” came into focus near the end of the sessions. “We needed a couple more songs for our album, and we took names out of a hat and split into two groups,” Starwood recalls. In one room, the three lead singers — Leppänen, Ward, and Avery — wrote a vocal part by reworking an acoustic demo that Avery had brought in. In another, the three remaining members put together an instrumental arrangement that’s slower and softer than most Chainsaw songs, and entirely enchanting.

“We spent the rest of the evening just jamming it,” says Starwood, who remembers holding down a synth note with one foot while her hands were busy on violin. “It came together in such a satisfying way.”

Last winter, as they were putting the finishing touches on the album, several of the bandmates met in the studio to record backing vocals for the song. A few days later, after speaking with some students back at the BRIT School, Cherry heard the new mix with those group vocals for the first time. “It was so full-circle,” the drummer recalls. “It was so sweet. Tears in my eyes.”

“Nosedive” remains a highlight at their live shows, and they generally save it for the last spot in the set list. “Billy Ward’s dad got him for Christmas a bubble gun in the shape of a pink chainsaw, and Vera always wields it in that song,” Starwood says.

At a recent hometown gig at London’s Electric Ballroom, they took that peak even higher by detonating a confetti cannon during “Nosedive.” “It was a big bang,” Starwood says. “It was really loud.”

That does raise a potential problem for their shows next year, which include another run of bigger U.S. clubs in New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Austin, and Washington, D.C. in February.

“I don’t know how you top bubbles coming out of a pink chainsaw and confetti,” Starwood continues. “We can’t do the same thing twice. Dancers, maybe?” Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage

“Pyrotechnics,” Ward says. “That’s the word of the year, 2027: pyrotechnics.”

#3225. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on DeWalt, Milwaukee, and Ryobi Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Yes, Home Depot has already launched its early Black Friday deals, offering deep discounts on major brands of cordless power tools. They also update their sales page on Thanksgiving Day and include Black Friday in-store-only doorbusters as part of their seasonal sales.

For most home tool sets, Ryobi is a solid, durable, and versatile brand. If you plan to use your tools occasionally for home maintenance, this is the best bang for your buck. For daily use or for larger DIY projects, DeWalt tends to be the next best option. These tools have more robust chargers and tend to stand up to more rigorous use than Ryobi tools.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. If you already have a cordless tool set and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something else they can use, a single tool deal might make more sense.

3 shows to watch after you finish binge-watching 'The Body'

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's only been a week since "The Body" came out on Netflix, but the Quinn Shephard psychological horror series has already made its mark, hitting the No. 1 spot on Netflix's Top 10 TV shows chart in the United States and worldwide.

The eight-episode coming-of-age series focuses on a group of 2004-era Catholic school girls (played by Kristina Bogic, Sara Boustany, Geena Meszaros, Sofia Wylie, and Shirley Chen, among others) who trigger mass hysteria in their conservative town after a drug-fueled Halloween night initiation ritual goes wrong.

The show's mix of psychological horror, religious satire and campy eroticism has clearly been a hit with viewers and critics alike (as of press time, it has an 86% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes). And if you want that kind of spooky fun to continue, here are three shows like "The Body" to watch next.

If you haven't yet been stung by the survival horror and dark humor of "Yellowjackets," now's a great time to catch up with the Showtime thriller. Not only does the series feature a similar mix of supernatural eeriness, schoolgirl drama, mass hysteria, and moral murkiness as "The Body," but "Yellowjackets" is also officially entering its fourth and final chapter beginning on November 20.

In case you haven't tuned in yet, the survival saga centers on a high school girls' soccer team as they try to survive in the remote Canadian wilderness after their plane crashes, following the group through two timelines: directly after the crash in 1996, and 25 years later, with the now-adult survivors attempting to reckon with dark secrets and unresolved trauma. That split timeline means we get an iconic cast of both industry vets—including Melanie Lynskey, Juliette Lewis, and Christina Ricci—and notable newcomers like Sophie Nélisse, Jasmin Savoy Brown and Sophie Thatcher.

In the "spooky teenager" genre, few names are as notable as Carrie White. But rather than give us a by-the-numbers send-up of Stephen King's famous teen heroine, Mike Flanagan's Prime Video miniseries modernizes the cautionary tale of what happens when a youngster is pushed too far by their peers, chillingly bringing the relentless scrutiny and casual cruelty of social media and smartphone culture into the fold.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Summer H. Howell stars as the sheltered titular teen, who has to juggle not only grieving the sudden, untimely loss of her father but also entering the merciless world of public high school and the discovery that she might just be in possession of mysterious telekinetic powers. Given that "The Body" took direct influence from King's original tale and Brian De Palma's 1976 film adaptation, it's no surprise that both that Netflix series and Prime Video's "Carrie" share similar themes of religious extremism, mean-girl viciousness, social isolation, and feminine rage.

If you're looking for more religious horror and cultish creepiness, you don't have to leave Netflix after finishing "The Body"; "Devil in Ohio" is, handily, on the same platform, an eight-episode miniseries adaptation of Daria Polatin’s best-selling book.

Where "The Body" revolves around the cult-like dynamics of a group of Catholic school girls, though, the latter thriller is set within a literal satanic cult, from which the young Mae (Madeleine Arthur) has desperately escaped with a pentagram carved straight into her back. As she awaits foster care placement, Mae finds shelter with hospital psychiatrist Dr. Suzanne Mathis (Emily Deschanel), whose family life and suburban world are turned upside down by the strange occurrences and ominous secrets that chillingly emerge upon the teen girl's arrival.

#3223. Kiss Finally Show Their Vulnerable Side in New Doc: ‘The Less Secrets You Have, the Freer You Are’

The first few minutes of the new documentary Kiss: End of the Road set up its next couple of hours. “We’re Superman with a guitar,” singer-guitarist Paul Stanley tells the camera. “Unfortunately, age is our kryptonite.” A few minutes later in the film, we see an exhausted Gene Simmons onstage at a 2023 gig in Manaus, Brazil, sweat dripping from his makeup as he collapses into a pile, catching his breath in a chair for several minutes. The scene was an inauspicious start to the first show of the final leg of the diehard rockers’ “absolute final shows.” The band’s manager, Doc McGhee, recalls in the film: “Paul said, ‘I’m out of here. I’m not gonna die up here.'”

When Stanley hears those words today, though, he smirks and spins them into a positive. He’s dressed down in a hoodie, sitting in his home office for a Zoom interview. “Seeing my brother Gene not only struggling but failing, I said, ‘That’s it,'” he recalls. “I said, ‘Regardless of what he wants to do, I owe it to him to pull the plug … certainly for the evening.'”

Simmons ultimately mustered the necessary strength to lift the 40 pounds of battle armor he was wearing and resume one of his signature songs, “Cold Gin.” After the show, in one of the stadium’s hallways, Simmons asks the cameraman, “Did you catch me throwing up?” which leads to McGhee conceding, “They’re showing their age.” Even though Simmons, Stanley, guitarist Tommy Thayer, and drummer Eric Singer were putting their all into performing tongue-waving, fire-breathing, ziplining, hard-rock hits like “Detroit Rock City,” “Lick It Up,” and “Love Gun,” rocking and rolling all night, let alone for a few hours, was beginning to look ambitious.

“If there’s such a thing as more than 100 percent humidity, it was there,” Simmons says today. He’s dressed entirely in black, including his baseball cap and sunglasses, to Zoom in from a solo tour stop somewhere on the Dakotas border. “Combined with very high temperatures approaching 100 degrees, you walk out and you’re just drenched. Stupid me, I didn’t drink enough liquids, so down I went.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Asked now what he thinks of Stanley’s impulse to pull the plug on the show, Simmons says, “Bitch, who do you think you’re talking to?”

Simmons and Stanley’s friendship remains brother-like, though, as one especially funny scene from the doc, premiering here exclusively, shows.

Simmons’ bravado about his rocky start in Brazil can’t overshadow the hard truths Kiss faced on the tour. The two-part doc, which premieres Thursday as a pay-per-view stream, occasionally feels like Spinal Tap: The band straightens out botched pyro cues, deals with a wardrobe malfunction when Stanley’s guitar gets hooked on his boot, and keeps playing while the streamers meant to burst out during “Shout It Out Loud” instead dangle from the rafters, floating down for hours. Stanley also contracted a bout of flu that forced the cancelation of three gigs in close proximity to the final show at Madison Square Garden.

Kiss had put decades into living up to their intro rap — “You wanted the best, you got the best” — but in the film they reveal how they faced long odds to make good on that claim in the lead-up to that MSG farewell show, which took place on Dec. 2, 2023. “These guys understood that for the film to be authentic, it had to be warts and all,” End of the Road’s director, DJ Viola, tells Rolling Stone via email. “Neither Gene nor Paul loved having a camera around during their lowest moments. Who would? But they understood why those moments mattered, and they trusted that the film would portray them honestly.”

Much of the documentary shows how hard Kiss work to get it right on the road, but longtime fans will be surprised to see how vulnerable their heroes appear. These are the guys who built their legend pouring their literal blood into the ink of a Marvel comic book, the guys whose hard-partying rock anthems influenced musicians as diverse as Nirvana, Pantera, and Garth Brooks. These are the guys who’ve plonked their logo on everything from condoms to caskets, the guys who kicked off a Farewell Tour in 2000 and refused to say goodbye. Related Content Kiss Take Their Curtain Call in New ‘End of the Road’ Doc Trailer At the 2026 Songwriters Hall of Fame, Even Legends Had Notes on the Music Business Ace Frehley’s ‘Budokan’ Guitar, Kirk Hammett’s ‘Black Album’ Ouija Guitar Go to Auction Kiss’ Paul Stanley Touts New Avatar Spectacular in Vegas as More Interactive ‘Antithesis’ of the Sphere

Now Stanley is 74 and wants to spend time with his teenage kids, while Simmons is three years older and just wants to play gigs without Kiss’ heavy baggage — literally. “I’m a huge Radiohead fan,” Simmons says, “but if Thom [Yorke] got into my outfit, as my Italian friends in New York would say, fuhgeddaboudit.”  Of course, they made it to MSG, and the movie gives a front-row view to why Kiss have (finally) retired from touring.

“There certainly was a long period of time where we projected invincibility and immortality,” Stanley says. “I think to humanize that now doesn’t weaken who we are. It actually strengthens it. I’m a big believer that the less secrets you have, the more free you are.”

Simmons is more guarded about what ended up onscreen. “The doc is really an interesting exercise in trying to figure out what to show, what not to show,” he says. “All in all, I think it’s pretty good.”

“Neither Gene nor Paul asked me to remove a single moment from the film,” says Viola, who previously directed A&E’s Biography: KISStory. “There wasn’t one scene that made it in or was left out because of a note from either of them.”

THE FILM’S MOST REVEALING moments show Stanley and Simmons weighing the future of their career, and like a few great Kiss songs, one of the most telling scenes takes place in the backseat of a car:

Stanley: Look, we were just offered a lot to continue.Simmons: We were?Stanley: Yes.Simmons: I like money.Stanley: I like pride.

Ultimately, pride won out — at least regarding touring. Other than special engagements like the band’s “unmasked” performance at its own Kiss Kruise: Land Locked in Vegas event this past weekend, the duo swear Kiss are done on the road. But there’s still plenty of money to be made.

Even if Kiss, the band, are done, the idea of Kiss will continue. Simmons, ever playing the role of rock’s answer to Don King, hypes a future that could include a Kiss cartoon, theme park, biopic, and the avatar shows they teased at their final show. Their multimillion-dollar rights deal with Pophouse positions Kiss, the brand, well.

The business can keep going, but as the doc shows, Stanley and Simmons had to learn to let go of the stage itself. “At a certain point we decided, ‘OK, this is the top,'” Simmons says. “It’s not going to get any better.”

Since 2004, Stanley has had both hips replaced, both rotator cuffs repaired, and he’s undergone repair surgery for torn biceps. Most recently, he had shoulder surgery in 2021. He reckons Kiss played some 250 shows on the End of the Road tour while he was in his early 70s. “There are no 72-year-old football players, basketball players, or boxers,” he says. “I’ve sustained all the same injuries [as athletes]. …  On that final tour, that was our peak, to me, in terms of the band, the technology, the camaraderie.”

Stanley also feels good about bowing out now since Kiss have achieved what he calls “the trifecta”: trophies from the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame (they sit behind him on a marble table as he speaks), as well as a Kennedy Center Honor. Although Kiss redefined hard rock for multiple generations, their makeup and carnival stunts made them something of a pop-culture novelty to rock’s gatekeepers until recently. But good things come to those who wait, and Simmons and Stanley waited long enough.

“Kiss is timeless because Kiss has always been very adamant about not singing about politics or saving the whales or anything of that sort,” Stanley says. “There are people or media to take care of that. We’ve always been about, dare I say, great rock & roll, entertainment, escapism, and self-belief, preaching that if we can do this, you can do this.”

That raises an obvious question: Could accepting the Kennedy Center Honor, presented last year by President Trump, who plunged the Kennedy Center into turmoil, be perceived as political? “Not at all,” Simmons says. “Fuck politics. The Kennedy Center Honors are highest accolades a civilian can get … I don’t care how people think of the president. He was elected by the electoral college. … It’s fair. If you don’t like it, vote somebody else in. But in the meantime, he’s the president. And if you don’t like the person, at least respect the presidency.”

Putting aside politics, Simmons believes the End of the Road tour was “as good as we could do, and it’s never perfect.” Both musicians mention the glaring absence at the final show of the band’s other founding members, guitarist Ace Frehley (who later died in 2025) and drummer Peter Criss. “It became impossible, which shouldn’t be a surprise to me at this point,” Stanley says. “When people have either unrealistic expectations or demands, you just have to decide: Either you acquiesce or you move on.”

Simmons says he personally asked them multiple times to participate but they declined. “Paul may have said it better than I did,” he says, “which is, ‘We wouldn’t have been here without Ace and Peter, but Kiss wouldn’t have existed with Ace and Peter.’

“Even today, I love Peter to death,” he continues. “We went to the Kennedy Center Honors, and we were all sitting together and, it was great looking at old times. But Peter and his wife complained enough that the Secret Service just abandoned them and said, ‘OK. We’re done,’ and they just walked off. This is the Secret Service.” (A rep for Criss did not reply to Rolling Stone’s request for comment.)

One former Kiss member whom Simmons didn’t bother inviting to the final show was Vinnie Vincent, the reclusive guitarist who recently resurfaced hoping to sell CD singles for $225 and an entire album for $2 million. “He was a talented guy, but damaged, in my view,” Simmons says. “He has yet to this day to sign his contract with Kiss. …  I wish him well. I wish everybody well. Life is short, and if you can get $2,500 for popcorn farts or whatever it is you want to do, God bless.”

Largely, the duo has few regrets about how the tour turned out. “Everything turned out the way it was meant to,” Stanley says. His only “minuscule” regret is that the band was a little hasty in unveiling in-production sketches of the avatars that will be part of Kiss’ ABBA-like show. He promises the real deal will be so much better.

“We see sketches, and Paul and I get in there and try to massage it and ‘Kiss-ify’ it,” Simmons says. Then he paints a vivid picture of how he sees the avatar shows looking: “Imagine virtual reality glasses,” he says. “You walk into a room, you’re in another dimension or dinosaurs are about to eat you up, all kinds of stuff. Now imagine seeing that reality without wearing glasses.”

“I’ll get old, he won’t,” Stanley says of the avatar. “Again, Kiss should transcend its inception and continue for decades to come in different forms, whether it’s ‘Kiss meets Scooby-Doo’ or the End of the Road Tour or Kiss Kruises, whatever it is. I was going to say it’s part of Americana, but it’s worldwide. We created something far bigger than us.”

WHEN STANLEY WATCHES End of the Road, he says he’s impressed by what he calls “the magnitude” of it. “We’ve always had a sense of responsibility to our legacy and to what people expect from us,” he says. “This was really a commitment by us to make sure that people felt validated and justified in their love for us.”

“For the first time, you get to witness the dedication, work ethic, obsessiveness, and love that goes into every single performance,” Viola says. But he also sees it as something more: “What this documentary captures is the last time Kiss brought thousands of people together in an arena to share that experience as one collective. There’s something incredibly powerful about that.”

In the years leading up to the final tour, Stanley became aware of what he calls “flaws in the armor.” Kiss are hyperaware of those sorts of shortcomings and don’t want to let their fans down. That’s clear in the film’s scenes of meet-and-greets and a fun one showing Stanley rehearsing his “People, let me hear you” and “Make some noise” cheers to an empty stadium before the show. “That’s me,” he says, shouting those same words out loud over Zoom. “That’s not an act.”

Simmons is happy to be done with the physical burdens of playing in Kiss. “I’m 77 now,” he says. “I’m doing OK. I got lots of hair — unfortunately, more on my ass and my back — but you have to know when to stop doing the thing that limits you physically, because I literally cannot do the same things we did when we were in our twenties. Neither can Paul. It’s just life.” Trending Stories Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’ John Mulaney Enlists Stepfather-in-Law's Country Band to Play 'Kimmel' The Lost Michael Jackson Tapes

Kiss have not broken up. Stanley describes Kiss’ next phase as “diversifying,” as they explore the upcoming avatar shows and what lies beyond. Simmons also says more music is on the way. “We actually secretly recorded a new song Paul wrote,” he says. “I can’t tell you more about it than that.”

“We’re not invincible, but [the idea of] Kiss is,” Stanley says. “Kiss is pretty much impervious to anything. But the people behind the band are human, ultimately — as much as we would like to think otherwise.”

Amazon's early Black Friday sale is bringing some pretty significant discounts on Apple devices, including several of the company's latest releases. The biggest savings are on the M5 MacBook Air, with up to $249 off, though there are plenty of smaller deals worth considering, too, from the AirPods Pro 3 at $179.00 to the Apple Pencil Pro at $99. You'll also find discounts on iPads, the Mac mini, and everyday accessories like the Magic Keyboard, Magic Trackpad, and AirTags. With Apple raising prices across its Mac and iPad lineups in June, citing higher memory chip costs, these sales offer a good opportunity to upgrade without paying full price.

The AirPods Pro 3 are down to $179 from $249, saving you $70 on Apple's latest premium wireless earbuds. They offer improved active noise cancellation over the previous generation, along with redesigned foam-infused ear tips and a heart-rate sensor that tracks workouts without an Apple Watch. They also support Live Translation with a compatible iPhone and carry an IP57 rating for sweat and water resistance. PCMag’s review goes into more detail on how they perform.

The AirPods Max 2, which launched in March, are already down to $449.99 from $549, saving you nearly $100 on Apple's premium over-ear headphones. The biggest upgrade over the original model is the H2 chip, which Apple says makes active noise cancellation up to 1.5 times more effective while introducing features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, and Live Translation. For more on its performance, check out this PCMag review.

The Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS, 42mm) is down to $329 from $399, saving you $70. It covers everything you'd expect from a premium smartwatch, including fitness tracking, health monitoring, notifications, and the ability to take calls when your iPhone is nearby. PCMag gave it an "outstanding" rating in its review and also named it its Gift of the Year for 2026.

If you'd prefer to occasionally leave your iPhone behind, the Apple Watch Series 12 (GPS + Cellular, 42mm) is $70 off, bringing its price down to $429 from $499. It has all the same features as the GPS model but adds cellular connectivity, allowing you to make calls, send messages, and stream music even when your phone isn't nearby (provided you have an active cellular plan).

For a more affordable option, the Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS, 40mm) is down to $199 from $249, saving you $50. It covers the essentials, including workout tracking, daily activity monitoring, and notifications, making it a practical choice if you don't need the Series 12's more advanced health features. Check out PCMag's review for a closer look at what you get for the price.

The Apple Watch SE 3 (GPS + Cellular, 40mm) is also $50 off, bringing its price down to $249 from $299. For an extra $50 over the GPS-only model, you get the convenience of making calls, sending messages, and staying connected without keeping your iPhone nearby, provided you have an active cellular plan. It's worth considering if you regularly go for runs, head to the gym, or step out without your phone but still want to stay reachable.

Apple released the M5 MacBook Air in March with 512GB of base storage, double the previous generation's, along with a faster SSD and an N1 wireless chip that adds Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Right now, the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air (512GB) is down to $1,249.99 from $1,499. For a closer look at the M5 MacBook Air's performance and features, check out PCMag's review.

If you prefer a more compact laptop but need extra storage, the 13-inch M5 MacBook Air with a 1TB SSD is down to $1,399.99 from $1,599, saving you $200. That's twice the storage of the base model, giving you more room for large files, photos, videos, and applications without having to rely as heavily on external drives or cloud storage. You still get the M5 chip, faster SSD performance, and Wi-Fi 7 support, all in a smaller, lighter design.

The M6 Mac mini is down to $949.99 from $1,099, saving you $149 on Apple's latest compact desktop. Its 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU can handle everything from everyday multitasking to photo editing and more demanding creative work, while the upgraded Neural Engine helps with AI-related tasks—Apple says the M6 delivers substantial performance improvements over the earlier M4 model, particularly for graphics and AI workloads. For more on how it performs in everyday use, check out PCMag's review.

The M4 iPad Air launched in March, and the 13-inch model is already down to $949.99 from $1,049, saving you nearly $100. Its M4 chip can comfortably handle demanding tasks like photo editing, digital illustration, and multitasking, while the 13-inch Liquid Retina display gives you plenty of room to work across apps. You also get 256GB of storage for your files and creative projects. For more on what to expect, here's PCMag's review.

If you need more storage for your creative projects, the 13-inch M4 iPad Air with 512GB is $100 off, bringing its price down to $1,149 from $1,249. That's double the storage of the 256GB model, giving you more room for large photo libraries, video projects, downloaded files, and apps without having to rely as heavily on cloud storage.

For those looking for something more powerful, the 11-inch iPad Pro with the M5 chip and 512GB of storage is down to $1,299.99 from $1,399, saving you nearly $100. Along with the faster processor, it offers an Ultra Retina XDR OLED display with ProMotion support for refresh rates up to 120Hz, making it particularly well-suited for creative work, video editing, and other demanding tasks.

The Apple Magic Keyboard with Numeric Keypad is down to $109 from $129, saving you $20 on a wireless keyboard designed primarily for Mac users. It pairs wirelessly over Bluetooth and can be recharged using USB-C. For a closer look at all that it has to offer, check out PCMag's review.

The Magic Trackpad is down to $130 from $149, taking $19 off an accessory that brings the Multi-Touch gestures and Force Touch pressure sensing of a MacBook trackpad to a desktop setup, across an edge-to-edge glass surface. It connects wirelessly over Bluetooth and has a rechargeable battery that lasts about a month between charges. You can read PCMag's full review to see how it stacks up.

The Apple Pencil Pro is down to $99 from $129, saving you $30 on Apple's most feature-rich stylus. It adds squeeze and barrel-roll gestures, haptic feedback, and Find My support to Apple's stylus lineup, and it pairs and charges magnetically along the side of a compatible iPad, including the M4 iPad Air featured above. PCMag's review offers a more detailed look at how it holds up in everyday use.

The Apple Magic Mouse is down to $59.99 from $79.99, saving you $20 on Apple's wireless mouse with a Multi-Touch surface that lets you swipe between pages and scroll through documents using simple finger gestures. It connects to your Mac over Bluetooth and has a rechargeable battery.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Among the deals listed here, the M5 MacBook Air with 512 of storage has one of the larger discounts at $249 off, bringing its price down to $1,249.99, from $1499.

For most people, the Apple Watch SE 3 at $199 is a good starting point, covering everyday fitness tracking, notifications, and essential health features without the higher price of the Series 12. If you want more advanced health monitoring and a more premium smartwatch experience, the Series 12 at $329 is worth considering.

With the holiday season just around the corner, I’m turning to Joanna Gaines for inspiration to get my home ready. The “Fixer Upper” star doesn’t disappoint with her recent Instagram post on styling a mantelpiece with a sweet gingerbread theme.

No mantelpiece? No problem! While I’m lucky enough to have one and will use her creative ideas to curate my own cute display, you can easily adapt the look to create gingerbread-inspired decor anywhere in your home.

In a recent Instagram post, Joanne Gaines sets to work styling a mantelpiece with decorative products available from Magnolia, the lifestyle and home brand she founded with her husband, Chip Gaines.

A post shared by Joanna Gaines (@joannagaines)

When you break it down into stages, creating this look at home is surprisingly simple, whether you splurge on the exact products Gaines uses or opt for budget-friendly alternatives. Here is how to achieve the style both ways.

Gaines starts by building the foundation of the design by intertwining three Real Touch Cedar Mix Garlands, $43 at Magnolia, with red berries (only available in-store). Once she’s happy with the “natural and whimsical” base, she tucks gingerbread houses throughout the greenery.

To make it extra special, she uses Lighted Gingerbread decorations that add a warm glow, mixing two different sizes to add depth and dimension to the display. You can grab the smaller Lighted Cottage Gingerbread House for $25 at Magnolia.

Of course, a festive mantelpiece wouldn’t be complete without a display of stockings for each family member. Here, Gaines uses Marble and Gilded Stocking Holders, $22 at Magnolia, to display her stockings. Rather than sticking to one design, she mixes up the prints for an eclectic look, blending plaid, velvet and winter tulip-printed designs. I love the richness of velvet, so I would personally opt for the luxurious Chanel Velvet Stocking in Winter Moss, $30 at Magnolia.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Even with the stockings up, Gaines hasn’t quite finished her display. The final touch is the Joyeux Noel Candle, $30 at Magnolia, featuring warm notes of cranberry, mandarin and clove — once lit, it will feel like Christmas has well and truly arrived.

I love decorating my home for the holidays, though between buying gifts and hosting, I try to keep a close eye on my budget. While I adore Gaines’ festive decor, I’ve been hunting for ways to get a similar aesthetic for less. Here are six budget-friendly Amazon finds that will bring that same holiday charm to your mantel.

This beautiful Red Berry Garland can be intertwined with a pine garland to create the backdrop for your mantel decor. It measures 8.9 feet and includes two hooks at either end of easy hanging. Besides decorating your mantel, it’s the perfect festive decoration to dress your table, or even your front door.

Drape this Real Touch Norfolk Pine Garland on your mantel with the red berry garland above. Plus, right now, when you buy this pack of two garlands, you can save 31%, so you can layer for a luxurious look.

Why buy one gingerbread house when you can buy a whole village? This set of three houses all includes warm LED lights, creating a cozy village scene when lit. With textured roofs and realistic icing, these pretty gingerbread houses look good enough to eat.

Rather than getting out your tool kit to hammer in a nail, you can hang your Christmas stockings from your mantel with these Christmas Stocking Holders. The set includes a reindeer, snowflake, snowman and Christmas tree hook. And if you don’t have a mantel, place them on a shelf or bookcase.

This elegant coordinated set of six Christmas stockings includes three designs. Two classic green-and-red plaid stockings sit alongside two green and two white velvet designs. All are finished with a feature bow and come complete with a dark green hanging loop.

There’s nothing like a real candle to help you embrace the festive spirit. When lit, this scented soy wax candle will enhance the room with the warming fragrance of cypress, eucalyptus and fig. However, take care where you place the candle when lit, and never leave it unattended when it’s burning.

#3220. 10 Shows Like 'MobLand' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Crime dramas often attract big stars, and MobLand is no exception. The Paramount+ series stars Tom Hardy as mob fixer Harry Da Souza, with Pierce Brosnan and Paddy Considine in supporting roles and Helen Mirren having a ball as the thoroughly evil matriarch of the Harrigan crime family.

While families are complicated in even the best of circumstances, that's especially true of the Family. After you've watched the recently released second season of MobLand, try one of these other shows mixing crime and family (or Family) drama.

Theo James plays army officer Eddie Horniman (a name mentioned as often as possible), heir to the Horniman estate (there it is again) who, upon the death of his father, is named the Duke of Halstead. He learns that his dad was tied to various criminal enterprises, and that his scouse brother is millions of pounds in debt to a drug dealer. What else is the dapper, military-trained Duke to do but learn to navigate the violent underworld while looking cool? You won't be surprised to learn that this British crime drama comes from creator/writer/producer Guy Ritchie, who also has a hand in MobLand. Stream The Gentlemen on Netflix.

Another series from Taylor Sheridan (the Yellowstone guy), this pandemic-era hit stars Jeremy Renner as Mike McLusky, head of a family that’s been keeping the peace, through means fair and foul, in the title's company town for decades. The "business" of the corrupt burg happens to be incarceration, and the McLuskys thrive when business is up, even if Mike has slightly different ideas about how to run things. The show deals broadly with systemic racism and inequality in the prison system, but mostly it's a modern-day western about bringing justice to a corrupt town. It will conclude with a fifth season, streaming in 2027. Stream Mayor of Kingstown on Paramount+.

A consistently compelling combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda: He's actually a man recently released from prison who takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed before anyone really has a chance to get to know him. It's all part of a complicated plan to reunite with his lover Ana (Ivana Miličević), and to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail—but the town is ruled over by various criminal factions, and being sheriff doesn't guarantee any kind of safety; rather, the opposite. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

MobLand creator Ronan Bennett previously made this acclaimed series that succeeds by maintaining a narrow scope—in this case, a single London council estate. Dushane (Ashley Walters) and Sully (Kane Robinson) are residents and drug dealers at Summerhouse, maintaining an increasingly precarious grip on the criminal element in the community. Most compellingly, the series maintains an extensive supporting cast of locals both in the drug trade and impacted by it, building a disturbingly compelling world. A little confusingly, the first couple of seasons were renamed Top Boy: Summerhouse when the show moved to Netflix, so you'll want to start there before moving on to plain ol' Top Boy. Stream Top Boy: Summerhouse on Netflix.

Based loosely on a nonfiction work investigating the Mafia-like Camorra in Campania, this show focuses on the head of the Savastano clan, Pietro Savastano (Fortunato Cerlino), and his ambitious lieutenant Ciro Di Marzio (Marco D'Amore). When Pietro is arrested at the series' outset, a civil war erupts between family members and among the factions vying for control. Gone are the suits and poker games of many a mob drama—this is a brutal, street-level take on organized crime that forsakes the typical trappings of the genre. Stream Gomorrah on HBO Max.

I'm here for the Pierce Brosnan of it all, but there's also a very strong vibe match in this series that casts the one-time James Bond actor as the head of a literal crime family, even if this one's set in the American West. Adapting Philipp Meyer's 2013 Pulitzer Prize-nominated novel of the same name, the series follows Eli McCullough, a ruthless cattle baron making moves to get in on the burgeoning oil industry in the Rio Grande Valley of 1915. A parallel narrative sees Eli as a young man, kidnapped and raised among a Nʉmʉnʉʉ family. While his backstory lends the character welcome complexity, in the present, he's as determined to build his empire as he is to prepare his son and grandson to take over when he's gone. Stream The Son on Prime Video.

Tom Hardy playing a tough guy isn't terribly unexpected, but here the setting is London, just after the end of the War of 1812. Hardy plays James Delaney, who returns from Africa after ten years away (he says he'd been taken prisoner, but his story doesn't entirely add up) for the funeral of his father. Dad left nothing but a little hunk of land off of Vancouver, not worth much until the war's conclusion creates new maritime trade opportunities. Suddenly, the United States, Great Britain, and the East India Company all have eyes on the real estate, and all are willing to do whatever it takes to acquire it—and the stakes become clear once James realizes that his father's cause of death wasn't natural. Stream Taboo on Peacock and Tubi.

Best not ponder too much on the fact that this one's based on a video game, as its pedigree is only hinted at via the levels of action and violence (certainly compared to some of the other shows on this list). Colm Meaney plays Finn Wallace, the absolutely indispensable leader of London's criminal underworld, a man who's been holding everything together for decades, until his shocking murder at the outset of the series (that's not a spoiler, and we spend more time with him via flashbacks). The completely random killing by someone who had no idea what he was doing begets chaos and open violence. Finn's son Sean (Joe Cole) has been raised to take his father's place, but local, Pakistani, and Albanian gangs all move in to take control from the Finn family in the power vacuum. Stream Gangs of London on AMC+.

The great Forest Whitaker stars as the real-life Bumpy Johnson, who returned from a prison sentence to find his neighborhood falling apart and in the grip of Italian mobsters. A more than capable crime boss in his own right, Johnson resolves to take on the Genovese crime family, eventually forming a tentative alliance with Malcolm X (Nigél Thatch and, later, Jason Alan Carvell). Johnson is the lesser evil as far as Malcolm and others are concerned, and a complicated figure as both crime lord and family man with aspirations of saving his neighborhood. The show will conclude with a two-hour finale, likely airing in 2027. Stream Godfather of Harlem on Hulu.

Adopted into an Italian organized crime family as a baby, Park Joo-hyung took on the name Vincenzo Cassano, eventually becoming a mafia consigliere. After his adoptive father Don Fabio dies, Fabio’s biological son comes gunning for his brother, whom he now sees as competition. Cassano flees to Seoul, on the hunt for a secret stash of money, and in the process discovers a love interest and a new adversary in a giant business conglomerate that definitely deserves to be taken down. An incredibly popular K-drama, this one definitely puts a unique spin on the tropes of the mob genre. Stream Vincenzo on Netflix.
