#3165. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

#3163. The Google Wallet app is now available on iOS

Google Wallet is now available on iOS to “organize purchases, tickets, boarding passes, and more in one easy place” in the US.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

The next tab shows a list of recent transactions associated with Google. The Wallet app will display purchase emails and summarize them. You also get a list of Passes, which you can pin/unpin from the homepage, and payment methods saved to your Google Account.

The ‘plus’ FAB (floating action button) lets you add loyalty, gift, and payment cards (for use in Chrome). There’s a convenient “Everything else” camera scanner that can be used to digitize anything else.

The other main reason Google Wallet now exists on iOS is that the company wants the app to be a “secure hub for managing agentic purchases across Google.”

As more reviews flood in, one thing is becoming clear: Rockstar looks to have delivered a game worthy of the wait.

If you’re counting down the minutes until you can play the game for yourself, I’m bringing you live updates on GTA 6 reviews and beyond. Plus, I’ve also found a selection of GTA 6 Black Friday deals if you want to upgrade your setup before playing for yourself.

Reviews are now live for GTA 6. Here's a selection of the scores:

Okay, so GTA 6 isn't launching on PC (I'm sure a PC port is coming in 2027), but the fine folks over at PC Gamer got their hands on an early copy and put together a report after 100 hours of gameplay. Writer Christopher Livingston was very impressed with the game but did note, "it will be (mostly) so much greater when it comes to PC." Maybe when GTA 6 arrives on PC, we'll get the 60 fps mode of our dreams!

Dave LeClair, Managing Editor, checking in. I was going to wait a bit for GTA VI, since the little time I get to play video games now is pretty much locked down by Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

However, after seeing these review scores, I might have a hard time waiting to get the biggest video game release of all time. I might have to jump on my Xbox Series X and plunk down the cash for a pre-order so I can get some time in this weekend.

So I turn to you, our readers, with a poll:

Midnight already felt so far away, but these reviews are making the wait feel extra long. Of course, some parts of the world are already playing GTA 6 right now! You can check how long you have left to wait via this nifty fan-made GTA 6 countdown clock. I've got 10 hours to go!

Those nominations certainly don't look undeserved now, based on the reviews that have just dropped. At this point, you would have to say that GTA 6 looks like the clear favorite to win GOTY.

More reviews have gone live, and as of writing, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game on Metacritic. It's at an astonishing 99 after 146 reviews. While the original Ocarina of Time also boasts a 99 score, that's from a much smaller sample size of just 22 reviews (it's a game from 1998, before the explosion in online game reviews). This score could change as more reviews are published, and post-launch reviews could be more critical, but so far, it's holding. GTA 6 really is getting unprecedented review scores.

If you had any doubts about pre-ordering GTA 6, these reviews might have swayed you. The game is getting perfect scores across the board, and is being described as "the game of the generation." You can still lock-in your pre-order, and if you opt for the "code in box" edition you get a free poster as well (and £5 discount in the U.K.).

Another five star review comes from Gamesradar. Reviewer Josh West writes, "GTA 6 is the highest-fidelity sandbox of its generation. Rockstar has built an open world of truly astonishing scale, scope, and quality. Another GTA 6 review, another perfect score. This time from Destructoid. Their reviewer, Scott Duwe, writes, "Grand Theft Auto 6 is part criminal come-up tale, part love story, and part life sim all wrapped up in an impossibly deep and detailed Rockstar Games open world that may never run out of things to do. For the last three-plus weeks, I have been gleefully vacationing in Vice City: robbing banks, fighting drug dealers, stealing cars, and enjoying the view while not coming close to finishing everything it has to offer. GTA 6 is finally here now, and it was well worth the wait."

Wow. As of writing, Grand Theft Auto VI holds a near-perfect 99 score on Metacritic. This would tie it with the best reviewed game of all time, the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Of course, this score could fluctuate as more review scores pour in, but the game is off to one heck of a start. Could this be the best reviewed GTA in history?

"Unprecedented. Unbelievable. Unmissable." That's the strapline for IGN's GTA 6 review. Quite a way to open any review.

I regularly find myself in love with video games, but it’s extraordinarily rare that I find myself in complete awe of them. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played."

Over on review site OpenCritic, GTA 6 is off to a flying start; it's currently got a 99 average score, with 100% of critics recommending it. Rockstar looks to have delivered and then some!

VGC's Jordan Middler says, "Grand Theft Auto 6 is a modern masterpiece. Rockstar's developers have created a remarkable open world that excels in storytelling, gameplay, visuals, music and technology to achieve something truly unmatched. Minor performance issues don’t dull the sparkle of an absolute must-play experience. GTA 6 was more than worth the wait." VGC has given GTA 6 a full 5/5!

GTA 6 reviews are going live, and the first one I've spotted is from Giant Bomb, their reviewer, Dan Ryckert, has given the game a full 5 stars, and said:

"Grand Theft Auto VI is Rockstar’s best game. In terms of inspiring awe at how far video games have come, I can only compare it to formative experiences of mine like playing Super Mario 64 or Metal Gear Solid for the first time. In the thirteen years between entries of one of the biggest franchises in entertainment, fans’ expectations grew to a level that felt unrealistic. Somehow, Rockstar has managed to overdeliver on the most hyped video game of all time."

Because of timezones, this means the lucky folks in New Zealand can enter Vice City first (I'm not jealous...).

Reminder, it's also been reported that GTA 6 reviews will drop as the game goes live in New Zealand, so we might be minutes away from getting our first critical impressions of GTA 6 as well. Should (hopefully) be lots to discuss very soon.

A big decision when it comes to GTA 6 is which version to get, the standard or the Ultimate Edition, which costs an extra $20, but comes with plenty of extra digital goodies. Let me know which edition of the game you've gone for in the poll above.

Other nominees for the event's top honor include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, 007: First Light, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem and Control Resonant. That's great company to be in, and it would suggest that GTA 6 won't disappoint! You can check out the full list of nominees here.

Of course, the single biggest question today is when exactly GTA 6 reviews will appear. Rockstar hasn't officially confirmed when critics will start delivering their verdicts on the game. However, a recent article from Insider Gaming claims that GTA 6 reviews are embargoed until today (November 18) at 3 a.m. PT / 6 a.m. ET / 11 a.m. GMT. That would mean GTA 6 reviews in less than an hour. But without word from Rockstar, this reporting should be taken with a grain of salt. It's not confirmed.

#3161. ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’: Could Video Game Franchise Become Film Or TV Show? “We’re Very, Very Selective,” Says Take-Two CEO

The world is currently being swept up by the latest Grand Theft Auto video game, but could the record-setting franchise one day be a TV series or movie? The answer, according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick: Maybe, in the right circumstances.

Prior to Grand Theft Auto VI breaking pre-sales records ahead of its official global release tomorrow, Zelnick was asked about “line extensions” for the gaming franchise during a recent appearance on The David Rubenstein Show podcast – to which he gave a measured response.

“We’re very careful about line extensions because this is a creative company and our goal is to make the best entertainment on earth – entertainment we’re always proud of,” said Zelnick. Related Stories Video Games 'Grand Theft Auto VI' Turns Chaos & Crime Into Cash & Clout With Record-Shattering Launch News Microsoft "Deeply Sorry" About Global Outlook Outage, Insists Disruption Caused By "Network Capacity Upgrade"

“We would make a movie or television show based on our intellectual property if our creative teams were passionate about it – if they thought they would somehow engage and delight our consumers. It’s a high bar to do that, and of course, there’s always a risk of failure. So we don’t rule it out, but we’re very, very selective.” Watch on Deadline

Jack Black has previous voiced a desire to appear in a Grand Theft Auto title or another Rockstar game, though Dan Houser, a key player in the franchise’s development, has previously warned a movie was unlikely to ever be made.

Top-selling video games have become solid bases for TV and film adaptations, with Netflix taking The Witcher to multiple seasons, HBO gaining critical acclaim for its version of The Last of Us and the likes of Super Mario Bros, Sonic the Hedgehog and Minecraft all having successful movies released in recent years. Elden Rings was recently being shopped at the American Film Market.

Grand Theft Auto, however, has never been adapted, perhaps due to its sprawling and wild nature and each game introducing new protagonists and cities.

Grand Theft Auto VI, which is the most expensive game ever developed, has taken an estimated $1.5B in pre-sales – far higher than any TV or film series in history and almost double the $800M Grand Theft Auto V bagged in 2013. Reviews have been universally superb, with its current Metacritic score placing it all-time joint first with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The sandbox game lets the player take control of two characters, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a Bonnie and Clyde-style couple in Leonida, an open world setting based on Florida. As the eighth main game in the franchise, its development took far longer than any of its predecessors, with a full 13 years between its launch and Grand Theft Auto 5.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. #3159. OpenAI upgrades ChatGPT and Codex with new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

Some of you have been asking very politely. Some of you have just been asking.GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available.Super efficient and built to perform where it counts—the real world.https://t.co/qr2iP0GpfX pic.twitter.com/jLCyVIws2Y

Both models are available starting today in ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu.

The $200/month Pro plan also gets Ultrafast mode for the first time with Sol. The $500/month Pro plan gets Ultrafast on both models, as do eligible Enterprise and Edu workspaces once an admin enables it.

How fast is Ultrafast? OpenAI says it can generate tokens at up to 4.5 times the standard rate on either model, although it uses more of your allowance. You can switch speeds from the model picker.

Developers can use both models through the API today as well. Astra’s standard input and output prices are 20% lower than with GPT-6 Astra, while Sol keeps its GPT-6.1 pricing.

You can read more in OpenAI’s full announcement.

#3157. Paris Hilton and AOC press the House to pass the Defiance Act on deepfakes

The Senate passed the Defiance Act unanimously in January, but the House has never voted on it. Paris Hilton says strangers have made over 100,000 AI deepfakes of her.

Paris Hilton, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Representative Laurel Lee at a Defiance Act press conference outside the US Capitol in January 2026

Paris Hilton and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez asked the House on Tuesday to vote on the Defiance Act. The bill would let victims of sexually explicit deepfakes sue the people who make and share them. The Senate passed it by unanimous consent in January. The House has never voted on it.

Hilton spoke on the steps of the Capitol alongside Ocasio-Cortez, Representative Laurel Lee and victims of deepfake abuse. She said strangers have made more than 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos of her.

“I can’t control who sees them. I can’t control where they go. And I can’t make it stop. And the laws aren’t protecting us,” Hilton said.

Her team also looked at how women in Congress appear in this content, she said. Of the 156 women in the current Congress, 83 have sexual deepfakes of them online, according to her team.

The Defiance Act would add a civil right to sue to existing federal law, CNBC reported. Victims could sue anyone who creates, shares, publishes or threatens to share such images without consent. They could also recover legal costs and ask a court to order the content removed.

The Take It Down Act, signed in May 2025, already makes sharing such images a federal crime. Platforms must remove them within 48 hours of a valid request. Critics say it leans on federal prosecutors and gives victims no civil route of their own.

The House version has 70 cosponsors, 35 from each party, CNBC reported. Microsoft, Snap and OpenAI are among its backers. House Speaker Mike Johnson called it “good policy” in September but said the House had not yet built consensus. If the House does not act before this Congress ends, the bill must be reintroduced in January.

Lawmakers elsewhere are also moving against nudify tools. The UK plans a law requiring Apple and Google to block nude images for children. In the US, the Justice Department has backed xAI against Minnesota’s nudify ban. Giorgia Meloni has filed to trademark her voice against AI copies.

“This is not a Republican or Democratic issue. This is a human issue,” Hilton said.

#3156. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

The new Marvel Comics app is a major improvement over Marvel Unlimited. Powered by Webtoon, this new mobile and desktop app gives you instant access to over 35,000 Marvel comic books, or over 85 years' worth of stories from The House of Ideas. While the new app isn’t perfect, it delivers easier navigation and a slicker interface than its predecessor.

I’m not familiar with Webtoon, but I used Marvel Unlimited for many years, as I detailed in my Marvel Unlimited — here's the 5 best classic comic books to read first article. I’ve used the Marvel Comics app for the past week and have largely enjoyed the experience. This is especially true because I haven’t read new Marvel comic books in a couple of years. The app provides a nice way to catch up where I left off — not to mention reading or re-reading the classics.

Here’s everything you need to know about the new Marvel Comics app, along with my hands-on experience using the app on some of the best tablets.

The new Marvel Comics app offers over 35,000 comics from the company's extensive catalog of Marvel, Star Wars, and 20th Century Studios. The Base subscription costs $9.99 a month or $69.99 a year, while the Ultimate tier costs $12.49 a month or $99.99 a year.

As Marvel detailed when it announced its partnership with Webtoon Entertainment for the new Marvel Comics app, Webtoon built the app from the ground up for mobile and web. Like the company’s own comic book reading platform, the Marvel Comics app lets you discover new and old books faster and makes reading more flexible across devices. The app supports traditional page-based comics (single-issue “floppies”) and vertical-scroll formats, such as Marvel Infinite.

The dynamic cover-scroll interface lets you browse comics right on the home screen and dive into the dedicated Discover section to find specific titles, characters, and creators. You can follow your favorites by clicking the follow button so you don’t miss new books or revisit older titles. The Pull List is especially useful because it surfaces the latest issues from followed series, characters, or creators. There is even an Upcoming Release section that shows which books will be available so you can add them to your Pull List ahead of release.

The Marvel Comics app offers two subscription tiers. The Base tier costs $9.99 a month or $69.99 a year (both plus tax). This gives you access to the full Marvel Comics digital library, with new issues arriving as soon as three months after their print release. The Ultimate tier gives you access to new comics as soon as 30 days after their print release, on top of the full library. This tier costs $12.49 per month or $99.99 a year (plus tax for both).

At first glance, the new Marvel Comics app doesn’t appear all that different from the old Marvel Unlimited app. As before, the interface has colorful comic book covers on a black background. However, the differences become apparent when you take a closer look at the dedicated sections on the Home page.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Continue Reading section is there as before and is self-explanatory. This lists up to 20 books, so you’ll have plenty of space if you’re reading a lot of them. The Pull List directly under that section shows ma the latest issues from the series, characters, and creators you follow. You’ll find many of these books in the Latest Comics section further below, though this latter one has all the latest issues even if you don’t follow them.

Beyond that, there are several sections featuring recommendations and guides based on what you follow, along with showcases for whatever’s the hottest thing at Marvel—which, at time of writing, is the new Midnight imprint.

I tested the app on the iPad mini 8, iPad Pro M5, Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, and on my iPhone 16 Pro Max. I found that the app was just as snappy and responsive on all of these platforms, which include iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and Android 17. The interface is slightly different on Android, with the Home, Explore, Library, and Account tabs residing at the bottom of the Home page instead of at the top like on Apple devices.

Though I’ve gotten used to it, I find the Home page somewhat cluttered. I think all of the recommendations and guides are fantastic for brand-new readers, but if you’re like me and mainly want to see the new comics, it can be a lot to sift through. This is something that the rival DC Universe Infinite app has mastered, as you get the latest releases and trending series up top and dedicated reading guides at the bottom.

I have mixed feelings about the Explore tab. While it does let you browse through specific books/characters/creators, I wish it were something more user-friendly than an alphabetical list of whatever you’re exploring. Sifting from Amazing Spider-Man to X-Men isn’t exactly streamlined, let alone engaging. That said, typing what you’re searching for (such as Daredevil) brings you to a page with guides and series that are easier to navigate.

Lastly, I wish there were a dedicated settings option so that I could change the background from black to white. Yes, this would make the app appear more like DC Universe Infinite and less "Marvel-y," but having the option would be good, as the all-black background can be eye-straining for me.

The actual reading experience is largely the same as before. No matter which device I read on, drawings and text appear sharp and vivid. Page swipes are fast if you’re reading a full page like I typically do. I don’t often use the guided panel view on tablets, but it’s essential when reading on the iPad mini or my iPhone, since my eyes aren’t what they used to be. When you finish a book, you can then read the next issue or something the app recommends.

The biggest upgrade for me is getting new comics one month after they release physically in comic book shops. Again, I’m trying to get back into Marvel comics, so I want to be as up to date as possible. I also don’t think it’s a coincidence that this app launched a little over a month after the first Midnight books shipped in October. It was certainly nice seeing the new horror-centric takes on X-Men, Fantastic Four, and Spider-Man.

While this is a nice upgrade, I can’t say I’m surprised that the highest tier of the Marvel Comics app offers new books a month after retail. Why? Because this is something the DC Universe Infinite app has offered for over a year. Now, I can be up to date on both of The Big Two’s comics, which is awesome.

It’s still early days for the Marvel Comics app, so I’m sure Webtoon will tidy it up over time. If we can get fewer recommendations on the home page, a more streamlined search function, and the ability to change the background color, I'd be a lot happier.

Now that Marvel Comics has a new CEO, I think it’s the right time to return to the house Stan Lee and Jack Kirby (and many other legends) built. If you prefer reading comics digitally, or don’t want to pay $4.99 for single issues, then the Marvel Comics app is an excellent way to read the latest from Marvel, not to mention revisit your favorite stories from the past.

The $69 Base tier costs the same as Marvel Unlimited’s used to, and is a great way to dive in. If you’re more serious about your comics, the $99 Ultimate tier is well worth it—and also $20 less than DC’s Ultra yearly subscription plan. But whichever tier you get, you’re getting your money’s worth.

#3154. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

Read more: iOS 27 revamps AirPods settings in a big way, here’s the new design

Which AirPods features in iOS 27 are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3153. Apple blames an internal update for its iCloud and Apple Pay outage

Apple Pay and iCloud reports spiked on Tuesday, and every service was back by early evening. The Apple outage is the latest in a week of US failures that officials say are not linked.

Greg Joswiak and Vanessa Trigub greet customers at Apple Fifth Avenue in New York in October 2026

Apple said an internal update caused Tuesday’s outage, which hit iCloud, Apple Pay, the App Store and other services. The problem was not a cyberattack, the company said, Reuters reported.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” Apple said in a statement.

By early evening, all systems were working normally again, according to Apple, The New York Times reported.

Users reported problems with Apple Pay and iCloud sign-ins on social media and on Downdetector, which counts user reports. Apple Pay drew about 2,300 reports in the US around 12:20pm ET, Reuters reported. iCloud reports peaked at about 1,800.

Apple confirmed full outages at Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare, the Associated Press reported. Apple’s retail stores worldwide also reportedly had problems that halted sales and in-person support, according to The Register.

The Apple outage came after a run of failures in the US. Microsoft blamed a dormant July defect for its Microsoft 365 outage last Thursday. On Friday, a router upgrade in Arkansas led to a nationwide ground stop of US flights.

On Monday, Chase blamed a software bug for problems at several US banks. United Airlines also had a system outage that held up departing flights for about an hour.

On Tuesday, the NSA’s classified internal network, NSANet, went offline too. The agency described it as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance”, The Register reported.

On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was not under systemic attack, The Guardian reported.

“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber-hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business that the failures came from security upgrades that took longer than planned or did not come back as expected. Fixes for the recent PHP flaws were one example, The Guardian reported. Senator Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee, backed that view.

Security experts told The Register that outages like these may now be routine. AI tools are finding old flaws faster, and companies are racing to patch them. Mike Wiacek, Stairwell’s chief technology officer, founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. The Register asked him if this is the new normal.

“The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in,” Wiacek said.

#3150. Senators balk at Duffy’s $50bn air traffic ask as FAA pauses routers

Ted Cruz doubts Congress will fund the full air traffic control plan, and Democrats want answers by Monday. An FAA official signed off the Arkansas work, The Washington Post reported.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks at NASA Headquarters in Washington in July 2025

Senate Republicans pushed back on Tuesday against Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s $50bn request to overhaul US air travel. On the same day, the FAA said it had paused installing the routers linked to Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford pitched the plan to Republican senators at their weekly lunch, Axios reported. The administration sent the formal request in a letter that morning. The $50.1bn plan has five roughly equal parts, including $10bn to modernise air traffic control equipment, according to the Associated Press.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Senator Ted Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee.

Cruz said the administration should first show it can spend the $12.5bn Congress approved last year. Senator John Kennedy said Congress would not hand over $50bn, but could pay to replace copper wires with fibre optics. He also faulted Duffy for raising the ask from $30bn after the ground stop. Senators Rick Scott and Jon Husted said airlines and other users should pay more of the bill.

Democrats are wary too. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said the administration does not know how to use the money it already has. Duffy said he hoped Congress would not “piecemeal” the request. He is still open to splitting it up, he said.

The FAA switched off the function behind the trouble on the Juniper routers where it began. It did the same on more than 60 other Juniper routers and paused new installations, it said in a statement. The Wall Street Journal first reported the pause, according to CNBC. Older Cisco routers, in place for 25 years, are running the network for now, AP reported.

Duffy said the FAA had recreated what happened at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site. He said 68 earlier installations of the same routers had worked well.

“But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet,” Duffy said.

He called claims that AI played a part “completely unfounded”, CNBC reported. The FBI is helping with the investigation.

Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee asked the FAA and the Transportation Department to explain the failure in a letter. They want answers by 23 November. The FAA plans to switch more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, the letter says. About 400 sit in place so far, and 69 of them are operational.

“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed,” the senators wrote.

Duffy has questioned the work of the contractor, L3Harris. But an FAA official oversaw, tested and signed off the Arkansas work eight minutes before the ground stop, The Washington Post reported. Asked for comment, the FAA pointed to Duffy’s remarks, in which he said L3Harris should “hire better minds”.

The ground stop and the weekend recovery cost the four largest US airlines $345m, Bernstein analysts estimated, according to AP. The ground stop came a day after the Microsoft 365 outage and three days before a software bug disrupted US banks.

#3149. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3148. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

#3146. Nebius CTO Danila Shtan says ideas matter again now that execution is cheap

Danila Shtan told the TNW Podcast that AI coding agents have him building prototypes again. The Nebius CTO also says the sovereignty debate is sometimes over-hyped.

TNW’s Cristian Dina (left) and Nebius CTO Danila Shtan at HumanX in Amsterdam, 24 September 2026

Asked what breaks first when a company grows as fast as Nebius, Danila Shtan gave a one-word answer: everything. The scale and the pace of growth test everything his team builds, all the time, the Nebius CTO told TNW.

“You start building, you have some expectations about the growth or the client’s needs or the performance they need, and they come to surprise you every day.” Danila Shtan, CTO of Nebius

Shtan described Nebius as a Dutch company and one of the largest AI clouds in the world. He spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at HumanX in Amsterdam on 24 September. That day he also joined a fireside chat on the main stage about making AI agents work at scale.

Earlier episodes featured Alexander Rinke of Celonis, Kristin Fracchia of Gamma, and Daniel Dines of UiPath. The full conversation is in the video below.

Nebius provides the infrastructure for training and running AI models and for building applications on them, Shtan said. He leads software development, so his team builds the software that runs on the servers.

“They need access to high performance computing, which is essentially the heart and the blood and everything of the current AI revolution, hype, whatever you call it.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Some customers spend hundreds of millions on the platform, he said. Others spend $50 to run a small slice of compute for half an hour of internal experiments.

Shtan’s team is about 500 to 550 people. His day is mostly talking to them, he said. He checks on projects and gives feedback when something goes very wrong. Nebius builds a platform, but it also builds data centres, which he called a parallel organisation.

AI coding agents have him building again. He can test an idea in hours or days and show the team a rough prototype instead of talking them through it. His thought process was always faster than his implementation skills, he said, and agents now take on that part.

A significant portion of Nebius’s customers are American companies, Shtan said. American customers use European capacity, and European customers use American capacity.

European governments talk about sovereignty as infrastructure, he said. The US government talks about models and capabilities. Large companies talk about not depending on a single model vendor. He called all of these angles correct.

“I feel like sometimes they’re over-hyped, and this is not good for anyone. It’s not good for business.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Nebius wants to be one of the most important independent AI cloud companies in the world, Shtan said. Much of today’s AI capacity sits with vertical players that own the chips, the data centres, the models and the apps. He wants alternatives at every layer, including model vendors and consumer apps.

“So we are all for diversity, and we are all for, like, building this independent layer of AI because too much power in one company’s hands, even if it’s a good company is never a good idea.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Its biggest challenge is growth, he said. Demand keeps rising for large, small and specialised models, and the bottleneck is no longer only GPUs. It is also memory, disks, servers, electricity, land and high-voltage equipment.

Shtan has been an engineering manager for about 25 years. He started as a software developer and moved quickly into managing people. He has worked in warehouse automation, retail, fintech, biotech, a news outlet and a classifieds website. Later he moved into developer tooling, clouds and Nebius.

For young builders, he said, this is a great time, because a large team is no longer needed to ship a successful product. Taste in product and the ability to sell it now matter more. Five years ago, he said, the maxim was that ideas don’t matter and execution does.

“Now, execution is quite cheap, so ideas matter again.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

Companies fail at AI when they treat it as magic, he said. His advice is to learn its limits, experiment, fail and try again.

“AI is not a magical thing. It’s a tool.” Danila Shtan, Nebius

#3145. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

#3144. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

#3141. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

To read WABetaInfo‘s full report, follow this link.

#3139. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3138. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos at Blue Origin in Cape Canaveral, Florida, in February 2026

Jeff Bezos said on Tuesday he was “heavily involved” in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond. He told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman that five finalists did full screen tests. Once the team watched them, the choice was clear.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob,” Bezos said.

Bezos spoke at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference. Vik Bajaj, his co-founder at the AI start-up Prometheus, joined him on stage. He also gave the Nvidia board advice on replacing Jensen Huang and shared new figures on Prometheus.

Amazon MGM Studios named Pattinson as the new Bond on Monday. Amazon bought MGM in 2022, and this is the first Bond casting under its control.

The team cut a large shortlist down to five finalists, Bezos said. Each did “real old-fashioned screen tests” of three scenes, in full costume, on real sets and with other actors. The group, director Denis Villeneuve among them, spent a couple of hours on Friday reviewing the tests. They made the final call that day.

At first the team leaned slightly against Pattinson because of his fame, Bezos said. They weighed picking someone less famous.

“But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond,” Bezos said.

Asked if Huang should return to Nvidia, Bezos said he did not know what happened in the board meetings. Huang said on Tuesday he would come back if asked. The board has ruled out his return.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said.

Outside CEOs in complex companies have a “vanishingly small chance of succeeding”, he added. Hiring one should be a last resort. Amazon’s own handover is no guide, he said, because it followed a plan that ran for years. Huang, he said, deserves admiration and respect “no matter what”.

Bezos said his AI start-up Prometheus has about 250 staff and has raised roughly $14.5bn. Prometheus has already put much of that into computing power. The company builds AI models for engineering and manufacturing, which he called “AI for atoms”.

Its tools have designed analogue chips and radios in 12 hours, he said. That work would take a team of 10 to 20 people six to nine months. Blue Origin, his space company, is testing the tools on two projects in a private trial with early customers. He gave no date for a public launch.

Elon Musk is merging his companies. Asked if he would do the same with Prometheus, Blue Origin and Amazon, Bezos called it a funny idea. He said he had “nothing to announce”.

He also defended his contacts with President Donald Trump, who he said “reaches out a lot”. Shutting business leaders out is a mistake, he said. Politicians who blame Big Tech for high living costs are picking a villain, he added. They should fix the root cause instead.

Alina Maria Stan builds connections that people actually feel. As co-founder and COO of Tekpon, she turns product intuition into real moment (show all) Alina Maria Stan builds connections that people actually feel. As co-founder and COO of Tekpon, she turns product intuition into real moments of discovery, shaping how teams find and adopt SaaS every day. Since 2020, she has led Tekpon’s brand voice, media strategy, and growth plays with a clear focus on human outcomes behind every metric. Before Tekpon, Alina followed curiosity across industries and countries. She was CEO of King Casino Bonus and led affiliate and brand strategy at Extremoo Media and Fable Media in Denmark, where she learned how to build partnerships that last. Early on, she sharpened her CRM and pricing instincts at K.H. ApS, always asking why customers choose what they choose. Her approach is rooted in more than a decade of international experience and two master’s degrees, one in Sustainable Consumption from the Technical University of Munich and one in Consumer Affairs Management from Aarhus University.
